Schools and movements

Structuralism

Breaking conscious experience down into its elements.

What does it propose?Psychology should describe conscious experience by breaking it down into its simplest elements, as chemistry does with matter, and find out how they combine.
What does it study?Sensations, images and feelings, and their attributes: quality, intensity, duration and clearness.
How does it study it?Experimental introspection: highly trained observers described what they experienced in response to controlled stimuli, without interpreting it or naming the object.
Who took part?Edward B. Titchener at Cornell University and his students, among them Margaret Floy Washburn, his first doctoral student. He drew, with some differences, on Wilhelm Wundt.
What remains?Rigour in describing experience, interest in attention and sensation, and the idea that psychology needs systematic methods.
What is debated?Introspection offered no way of settling disagreements between laboratories. It left out children, animals, behaviour and disorders. It all but vanished with Titchener's death in 1927.

Context

At the end of the nineteenth century psychology had just split from philosophy and wanted to resemble the natural sciences. The Englishman Edward Bradford Titchener (1867–1927), trained at Oxford and in Wundt's laboratory in Leipzig, arrived at Cornell University in 1892 and built a very ambitious programme there: a "periodic table" of the mind.

Key ideas

  • Three kinds of element: sensations (from the senses), images (from ideas) and affections (pleasantness and unpleasantness).
  • Attributes: each element has quality, intensity, duration, clearness and sometimes extension.
  • The stimulus error: saying "I see an apple" was a methodological mistake. One had to describe colours, shapes and brightness, not the object.
  • Pure psychology: Titchener distrusted applied psychology and testing, which he regarded as technology rather than science.

An example

In a typical experiment the observer heard a tone and had to report its pitch, loudness, duration and how clearly it appeared in consciousness. Titchener catalogued more than 44,000 distinct sensory qualities, about 32,800 of them visual and about 11,600 auditory.

Historical importance and current support

Historically it mattered because it forced psychology to define its methods and because its critics, the functionalists and behaviourists, built their proposals in opposition to it. Today it has no followers as a school. But some of its questions are still alive: modern psychophysics measures sensations precisely, and research on consciousness once again uses verbal reports, though with far more careful controls.

Titchener presented his programme as a continuation of Wundt's. Historians have shown that Wundt's thought was considerably broader, with a strong interest in will and culture.

Wundt and Titchener were not the same

For decades textbooks presented Titchener as Wundt's faithful successor. Historians such as Thomas Leahey and Kurt Danziger showed this was not so. Wundt gave great weight to will and attention, and devoted ten volumes to his Völkerpsychologie (folk psychology), on language, myths and customs, which could not be studied in the laboratory. Titchener focused almost exclusively on the elements of consciousness.

A laboratory without women

In 1904 Titchener founded a group of experimental psychologists, "the Experimentalists", which excluded women from its meetings until after his death. Christine Ladd-Franklin, a mathematician and psychologist, wrote to him for years in protest. Paradoxically, Titchener supervised many women doctoral students, among them Margaret Floy Washburn.

What introspection did teach

Although analytic introspection was abandoned, the idea of asking people about their experience did not disappear. Today methods such as experience sampling are used, in which a prompt asks people to describe what they are experiencing at that moment, with controls to reduce bias.

A school's historical importance and the current scientific support for its ideas are different things: we explain them separately.
